title: The four rounds
hookLine: he writes the four lavan, the wedding hymns that Sikh couples still walk around the Granth to (Suhi, ang 773)

lines: A MORNING WEDDING IN THE GURDWARA.
cards: If you've been to a Sikh wedding, you've seen it. Morning, in the gurdwara. The couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture, on its raised seat.

The bride holds one end of a long scarf, the groom the other. The musicians begin to sing, and the couple stands and walks slowly around the scripture, clockwise, the groom a step ahead, the scarf between them. They sit.
The singing starts again. They walk again. Four times in all.
Every round is a hymn, and all four were written by the orphan from Lahore, Guru Ram Das.

teach.b: They're called the lavan, the rounds. The hymn is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, with four stanzas, one for each round. Each describes a stage, in paraphrase.
The first: the duties of a good life, following the Guru's teaching, living honestly, remembering God's name.
The second: meeting the true Guru; fear falls away, and the mind is humbled. The third: the heart fills with longing and love, detached from the world's pull.
The fourth: the mind is at peace, and the soul and God are united as one.
Sikhs hear the lavan as two marriages at once. On the surface, a husband and wife walking into a shared life. Underneath, the soul's marriage to God, the union the hymn keeps singing toward.
So the couple isn't only promising themselves to each other; together they walk the soul's path, round by round, with the scripture at the center.

teach.h: THE ANAND KARAJ, CEREMONY OF BLISS.
teach.b: The wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Remember Anand? It's usually closed with the Anand Sahib.
Now look back over the week. The baoli, water for all. The row, even for an emperor.
The manji, and she is not lesser. Anand, the song of bliss. Jetha the orphan.
And now four rounds, one life. Two Gurus, one idea running through them: everyone at the same level, walking the same path, with the Word in the middle.

how: In the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, the couple walks four times clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib as each of Guru Ram Das's four lavan is read and then sung, joined by a scarf.

practice: Think of a promise you keep, not one you've broken: to a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Remember when you made it, and every time since that you've kept it, round after round.
If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, just feel how long you've carried it.
